 Look, I like HiFi sound as much as anyone. Exacting headphones and speakers that really get to the bottom of the artist's intent, revealing details that most could only dream of hearing. Sometimes, though, after a long, hard day, I just want something that shakes my skull with all the low stuff. A speaker that doesn’t care about giving me an analytical presentation. Something that forgoes all pretense — a bassy speaker. Sony has done just that with the ULT Tower 5, a monster of a Bluetooth speaker with a peak output of 300W. That’s more than some dedicated HiFi amps. And it does it all with some fun LED lights and handles to carry it around a party. What more could I ask for?
 That’s not to say there’s only the bass going for the ULT Tower 5, far from it. Sony has managed to produce a sound profile that doesn’t just give all the low stuff but plenty of the rest of the frequency range too. Highs are good, and the mids are well-rounded. It’s a jack of all trades as well as a master of one — something not to be taken for granted. We were most impressed with the soundstage, though, which was wide and expansive when we did our testing. And we don’t mean just “ooh, it filled a room” type expansive; we mean solid stereo effect that makes it feel like you’re in the room with the band.
 But you don’t just buy a Bluetooth speaker for the sound — there’s everything else to worry about as well. And Sony has thought of “everything else,” up to and including the kitchen sink. The handles are a great addition to make it easier to lug from house to car to house party and back, and there are even some useful physical buttons on the back for playback and simple settings should you not want to pull your phone out.
 There are a couple of drawbacks, however. There’s the aforementioned IPX4 limitation, which is a bugbear more than a problem. It’s a heavy, heavy thing at 28lbs, making those carry handles all the more useful. Perhaps the most pertinent is the price. While it’s a lot of speaker for $450, it's still a lot of money to demand from an audience that is still reeling from the last bit of their student paycheck they had to launch at a new textbook for class.
 But when you finally get the money out of Mom & Dad, this is a monster of a speaker that’ll power and bassy gathering with ease. The bass is truly window-shaking, and the features are plentiful — just be ready for the neighbours to come a-knocking when things get unruly.

 How to choose the best speaker for you 
 Battery life 
 Battery life is a very important part of any new device that you choose. We've got some strict criteria on the battery life front — Wi-Fi speakers should get at least 10 hours, larger Bluetooth speakers should get around 20. This will depend on size, but you should be looking around those figures.
 Voice control 
 Some speakers you’ll find out there have voice control, or support for assistants like Alexa. Sonos is amongst the top, although there are speakers from the likes of Bose that also feature smart voice support. If you plan on using your speaker in a garden, or if it's going to be placed somewhere slightly out of reach, then being able to command it to play, pause, skip or select a new track could be useful. If its going to be nearby, or you’re going to have your phone within reach more often, then it’s not so necessary.
 Power output 
 When you look at Bluetooth speaker specs, there are often some confusing specs. You might see power figures like ‘Wattage’, frequency response numbers, and more. They can be useful, but they’re often inconsistent between different brands and testers, often only useful to the most dedicated of audio fanatic. If you’re just looking for a Bluetooth speaker, however, they’re not going to tell you much unless you do hours and hours of research.
 We test all the Bluetooth speakers that come across our testing tables in a number of different real-world environments so that we can tell you what the manufacturers' numbers might not. We make sure that we give you just what you need to know, testing the speaker where we think it is most likely to be used. A large, living room speaker gets tested indoors in different rooms for example, while a rugged, adventure model makes its way to the great outdoors. We look out for strengths and weaknesses in the three main frequency groups — bass, mid-range, and treble — so that you get a holistic view of how your music is going to sound.
 Price 
 For many people, the price of the Bluetooth speaker is what’s going to make or break the purchase of a new device. To get the very best speaker we’d recommend spending a little more on something from a well-known, established brand, because they often use more experience in creating something more successful. There are some great budget options if you’re looking for the best cheap Bluetooth speaker, of course. There are even some great cheaper options on this list.
Don't forget to bookmark our tech deals pages to keep on top of all the best Bluetooth speaker bargains.
 How we test the best Bluetooth speakers 
 At Tom’s Guide, we want to make sure that every speaker we test puts its best foot forward. While we test with strict criteria that each model must meet, we consider who, and what, it might be best for. While a speaker might not match up as a critical listening darling, sitting in the living room, it might be perfect for trips outdoors. We spend hours over the course of testing listening to music in different environments to make sure we get a good picture of the speaker's performance when we pen our detailed, informative reviews.
 The most important part of any speaker is its sound quality, and we listen to loads of tracks across a variety of different genres to evaluate the sonic performance of the speaker. We play everything from hip-hop, rock, and Jazz all the way through to heavy metal and classical to get the best idea possible of the kind of sound quality we’re working with. If applicable, we even try out movies and podcasts to get a holistic view of sound performance.
 We test durability, within reason of course, to make sure that the speaker is going to withstand the kind of everyday use you might expect. If the speaker has smart features, we make sure to evaluate voice assistant performance, and how it stacks up to the competition. We test how it might control your smart home devices as well, and how easy it is to play playlists with nothing more than your voice.
 We also look at battery life, completely draining the battery twice and recharging to see how it lasts with normal, expected use. We want good battery life out of these devices: Wi-Fi-connected speakers should be getting 10 hours, while Bluetooth (depending on their size) should be getting 20 hours.
 We rate the best Bluetooth speakers with our five-star system. A 1-star review is a complete waste of time, and should be avoided at all costs. A 2-star score is indicative of a product that works, and no more than that. A 3-star review is a fine product, although there are better options out there. A 4-star device is a good product, and while there are other options, it’s a great purchase. A 5-star score is reserved for the very best of the best. The almost perfect devices that work better than everything else around, and should be at the top of your potential purchase list.

 If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers , but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.
 Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150) , but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.
 Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars , Best Wireless Earbuds , and Best Computer Speakers .
 Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501, JBL Go 5, and Soundboks Rider to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information. 
 How I Test Bluetooth Speakers
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.
 Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.
 Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.
 I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.
 And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.
 What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?
 AccordionItemContainerButton 
 That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.
 As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.

It sounds remarkably good for something this compact (and affordable), with plenty of bass and punch, clear vocals, and refined detail. Build quality is excellent too, with IP68 water and dust protection and some drop-proofing (within reason)..
 JBL keeps improving the Flip with every iteration. It now has 14 hours of battery life (or 16 with the bass-reducing Playtime Boost mode), and Auracast lets you link newer compatible JBL speakers together for a surround sound experience. The app also has a useful seven-band EQ if you like to tinker with your tones.
 As a nice bonus for those who care about bit rates, the Flip 7 can play 24-bit/96kHz lossless audio if you plug it into a source via the USB-C, which is a surprising extra feature at this price point. JBL continues to be the brand to beat in the land of Bluetooth speakers.

 Wi-Fi connectivity means access to the full Sonos ecosystem and app, including more than 100 streaming services, voice control, automatic Trueplay tuning, and multiroom playback. Leave it on the supplied charging base and it’s a great Sonos speaker. Pick it up and switch to Bluetooth, and you have a portable speaker with a huge 24 hours of battery life and IP67 protection.

 The already excellent JBL Go 4 is a little cheaper, but the Go 5 brings fuller, deeper bass, clear mids, and enough punch to make music sound good. It’s not "serious" hi-fi, but the design and attention to detail—the tactile, spring-loaded, knurled metal power lever, and illuminated control knobs are a joy—stand apart. It just looks fantastic, and with 50 watts of power and 50 hours of playtime, it plays loud and long. I love being able to charge devices from the speaker’s USB-C port too.

 JBL Charge 6 for $150 : It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.
 Bose SoundLink Plus for $269 : Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.
 Sonos Roam 2 for $179 : The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.
 Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200 : If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata . It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.
 Beats Pill for $150 : Remember the Beats Pill ? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.
